newsitem.title: GHANA: Big rush for Ghana's first corporate bond.
newsitem.headline: Big rush for Ghana's first corporate bond.

text.p: Investors scrambled for Ghana's first registered corporate bond when it was offered by mortgage lending company Home Finance Co Ltd (HFC) on Wednesday.
Eight minutes after the offer officially opened at 0900 GMT, $150,000 worth of bonds were sold, said Ken Ofori-Atta, chairman of lead manager Databank Financial Services Ltd.
"We feel strongly that the offer will be oversubscribed. Fortunately HFC has agreed an over-allotment," Ofori-Atta said.
"This is the beginning of the organised corporate medium- to long-term bond market in Ghana," Yeboa Amoa, managing director of the Ghana Stock Exchange, told Reuters.

The $2 million, five-year bond, demoninated in dollars and yielding seven percent, will be the first corporate bond to be listed on the Ghana Stock Exchange, HFC's managing director Stephanie Baeta Ansah told a news conference on Tuesday.
The offer, closing on October 18, was targeted initially at insurance companies and multinational firms with local provident and pension scemes for their employees, Ofori-Atta said.
However, non-governmental bodies who want to put their savings in the local cedi currency into the bonds to hedge against depreciation had unexpectedly shown keen interest.
"We are very proud to be the first apex mortgage finance institution in Africa and the first in Ghana to issue housing bonds for listing on the local stock exchange," Ansah told Reuters.
"HFC is a good vehicle for launching Ghana's long-term debt project. Long-term funds are crucial for development, without which our economy cannot grow," she added.
Ofori-Atta said the bond was attractive "because of the soundness of the instrument and because it offers the possibility of hedging."
Ghanaians can now bring their cedis into an instrument that will secure the long-term value of their money, he said.
The bonds can be paid for in cedis and the exchange rate will be determined at the close of the offer. Bonds may be redeemed after two years.
HFC is Ghana's top mortgage institution. Six years ago it became the implementing agency for a $25 million housing finance scheme funded 60 percent by the state and 40 percent by the World Bank.
It has used other local funds to finance dollar and sterling denominated mortgages for Ghanaians working abroad and wanting to build in Ghana, Ansah said.
"That portfolio of mortgages was financed from our own working capital, shareholders' funds, pre-payments from our mortgages, repayments, and deposit accounts," Ansah said.

"We have to refinance that portfolio. Money here has become too expensive because of extremenly high interest rates and inflation. We need to hedge against what is happening on the market, even though I believe the situation will improve after the elections," she added.
Presidential and general elections will be held in Ghana on December 7.
Central Bank interest rates are at 46.88 percent for 91-day Treasury Bills. July year-on-year inflation was 42.6 percent.
HFC expects to issue more bonds and has already carried out shelf registration for a total of $35 million, Ansah said.
